# Screens before bed: what they cost your sleep

*Test fixture written for this repo. The numbers are illustrative.*

Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night. Many get less, and evening screens are one reason.

Light from phones, tablets and laptops delays the body's release of melatonin, the hormone that tells you it is time to sleep. Scrolling also keeps the mind busy. In one study, each hour of screen use in the hour before bed was linked to about 20 minutes less sleep that night. People who use screens in bed also take longer to fall asleep: around 15 minutes longer on average.

The loss adds up. If you lose 30 minutes a night, by the end of a working week you are two and a half hours short. Researchers call this sleep debt. A weekend lie-in pays back only part of it.

Many people think a dim screen or night mode solves the problem. It helps a little, but most of the effect comes from staying engaged, not from the light alone. Putting the phone away is what makes the biggest difference.

What can you do? Stop screens 30 to 60 minutes before bed. Keep the phone outside the bedroom. Read a paper book, or listen to something calm instead. Going to bed at the same time each night also helps, because the body learns when to wind down.

Sleep needs differ from person to person, and stress, caffeine and noise matter too. If you sleep badly for weeks, talk to a doctor.
